10.01.title: Systems, states and properties
10.01.html:
Thermodynamics is the science of energy and its conversions: fuel into motion in a scooter engine, electricity into heat in a heat pump, falling water into electricity in an Alpine power station. Its first rule of method is to say exactly what you’re analysing. Draw a boundary around it, decide what can cross that boundary, and describe what’s inside by a few numbers. Get this step wrong and every equation afterwards will be wrong too.

Systems

  • A closed system contains a fixed mass. Energy can cross its boundary as heat or work, but matter can’t. Gas in a piston-cylinder is the classic example; the boundary may move.
  • An open system or control volume has mass flowing in and out: a turbine, a pump, a nozzle, a heat exchanger.
  • An isolated system exchanges nothing at all with its surroundings.

Properties and states

A property is any measurable characteristic: pressure p, temperature T, specific volume v=V/m, internal energy u, enthalpy h, entropy s. Intensive properties don’t depend on size (p, T, v); extensive ones do (V, U, m). Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property.

The state is the condition described by the full set of properties. A process takes a system from one state to another.

The state postulate

For a simple compressible substance (no electric, magnetic or surface effects), two independent intensive properties fix the state. Everything else follows from the equation of state and property relations. For an ideal gas,

pv=RT,

so p and T give v. Specifying a third property over-determines the state: it must agree with the first two or the data are inconsistent. (Inside the two-phase region p and T are not independent, 10.06.)

Thermodynamic properties depend only on the state, not on how you got there. Heat and work are not properties: they depend on the path (10.03).

Worked exampleAir as a state object

Air as an ideal gas: R=287 J/(kg K), cp​=1005 J/(kg K).

  1. p=101.325 kPa, T=288.15 K: v=287⋅288.15/101325=0.81618 m³/kg, so ρ=1.2252 kg/m³, the standard sea-level air density.
  2. Specifying T and v instead gives back the same pressure.
  3. Specifying p, T and v=0.9 m³/kg is rejected: pv=91192 J/kg but RT=82699 J/kg.
  4. Specifying only T is rejected: one property doesn’t fix a state.
  5. At 2 MPa and 700 K, with reference 298.15 K: h=1005(700−298.15)=403.86 kJ/kg, and h−u=RΔT, consistent with h=u+pv.

10.02.title: The ideal gas
10.02.html:
Pump up a scooter tyre and the pump barrel gets warm. Leave the tyre in the Bali sun and its pressure rises. Both follow from the simplest and most used equation in thermodynamics, the ideal-gas law. It holds well for air, nitrogen, helium and combustion gases at ordinary pressures, and you can derive it by imagining molecules as tiny balls bouncing off the walls.

The equation of state

pV=nRu​T=mRT,pv=RT,

with Ru​=8.314 J/(mol K) the universal gas constant and R=Ru​/M the specific gas constant (287 J/(kg K) for air, M=28.97 g/mol). In molecular terms, pV=NkB​T with kB​=1.381×10−23 J/K.

Where it comes from

Consider N molecules of mass m in a cube of side L. A molecule with velocity component vx​ hits the right wall, reverses, and delivers momentum 2mvx​. It returns every 2L/vx​ seconds, so its average force on the wall is mvx2​/L. Summing over all molecules and dividing by the wall area L2:

p=VNm⟨vx2​⟩​=3VNm⟨v2⟩​.

Comparing with pV=NkB​T shows what temperature is: the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules,

21​m⟨v2⟩=23​kB​T.

The rms speed is 3kB​T/m​: about 517 m/s for nitrogen at room temperature, faster than sound.

When is a gas ideal?

The derivation assumed molecules take up no space and don’t attract each other. That’s good when the gas is far from condensing: low pressure, high temperature compared with its critical point. Steam near saturation and refrigerants are not ideal; 10.06 and 10.16 cover them.

Worked examplePressure from collisions

2000 nitrogen molecules in a cube of side 100 nm, with Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities, bounce elastically off the walls for 4000 time steps. The momentum delivered to the walls, divided by wall area and time, is the pressure.

  1. At 300 K (the sample’s kinetic temperature is 293.7 K): simulated 8111.6 Pa against NkB​T/V=8111.0 Pa, ratio 1.0001.
  2. At 200 K and 600 K the ratio is also 1.0001: pressure is proportional to temperature.
  3. The rms speed of N₂ (molecular mass 4.652×10−26 kg) at 300 K is 3kB​T/m​=517 m/s.

Exercise 1A scooter tyre in the sun

A tyre is inflated to 200 kPa gauge (301 kPa absolute) at 25 °C. In the sun it reaches 55 °C at constant volume. What does the gauge read?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At constant V and m, p∝T: p2​=301⋅328.15/298.15=331.3 kPa absolute.
  2. Gauge: 331.3−101=230 kPa.
  3. Always use absolute temperature and pressure in the gas law.

10.03.title: Work and heat
10.03.html:
Squeeze the air in a bicycle pump and you push the handle through a distance against the pressure. That’s work, the same force times distance as in mechanics. In thermodynamics we write it in terms of the gas’s pressure and volume, and it turns out that the amount of work depends on how you squeeze, not just where you start and end.

Boundary work

A gas at pressure p pushes on a piston of area A with force pA. Moving the piston by dx changes the volume by dV=Adx and does work pAdx=pdV. For a slow (quasi-equilibrium) process:

W=∫V1​V2​​pdV.

With the sign convention used here, W>0 when the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, and W<0 for compression. On a p-V diagram, W is the area under the path.

Common processes

  • Isobaric (p constant): W=p(V2​−V1​).
  • Isothermal ideal gas (pV= const): W=p1​V1​ln(V2​/V1​).
  • Polytropic, pVn= const with n=1:
W=1−np2​V2​−p1​V1​​.

n=0 is isobaric, n=1 isothermal, n=k=cp​/cv​ (1.4 for air) is reversible adiabatic, and n→∞ is constant volume (no work).

Heat

Heat Q is energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference. Like work, it’s a transfer, not something a system contains. Both depend on the path, which is why we write δQ and δW for small amounts rather than dQ: they aren’t changes of a property.

Worked exampleCompressing 10 L of air to 2 L

Air at 100 kPa and 300 K (11.614 g) compressed from 10 L to 2 L:

  1. Isobaric at 100 kPa: W=100000⋅(−0.008)=−800.0 J.
  2. Isothermal: W=1000ln0.2=−1609.438 J. Numerical integration of pdV gives the same to 10−3 J.
  3. Polytropic n=1.3: p2​=810.3 kPa, T2​=486.2 K, W=−2068.855 J.
  4. Adiabatic n=1.4: p2​=951.8 kPa, T2​=571.1 K, W=−2259.135 J. The steeper the path, the more work it takes, because the gas heats up and pushes back harder.
  5. Two rectangular paths between the same end states take −800 J and −7615 J. Work depends on the path.

Exercise 1A pump stroke

A bicycle pump compresses 0.5 L of air at 100 kPa to 0.1 L so quickly that it’s adiabatic (n=1.4). Find the final pressure and the work input.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. p2​=100⋅51.4=951.8 kPa.
  2. W=(p2​V2​−p1​V1​)/(1−n)=(951.8⋅0.1−100⋅0.5)/(−0.4)=(95.18−50)/(−0.4)=−113.0 J.
  3. You do 113 J of work on the air, and it ends up much hotter. That’s why the pump barrel warms up.

10.04.title: The first law for closed systems
10.04.html:
Energy can’t be created or destroyed, only converted. In mechanics that meant kinetic plus potential energy stays constant without friction. Thermodynamics extends the bookkeeping to heat and internal energy, the energy of the molecules' random motion. It’s the first law, and every energy calculation you’ll ever do, from a pressure cooker to a power station, is an application of it.

The first law

For a closed system going from state 1 to state 2:

Q−W=ΔU(+ΔKE+ΔPE),

with Q the heat added to the system and W the work done by it. In differential form, δQ−δW=dU.

U is a property: its change depends only on the end states. Q and W depend on the path, but their difference doesn’t. Over a full cycle the system returns to its start, ΔU=0, so

∮δQ=∮δW:

a cycle’s net work equals its net heat input.

Internal energy and enthalpy of ideal gases

For an ideal gas, u depends only on temperature: du=cv​dT. The enthalpy h=u+pv is also a function of T only, dh=cp​dT, with cp​−cv​=R. For air near room temperature cv​=718 and cp​=1005 J/(kg K).

At constant pressure, heat added equals the change in enthalpy: Q=ΔU+pΔV=ΔH. That’s why enthalpy appears whenever pressure is held fixed, or whenever fluid flows (10.05).

Solving problems

  1. Choose the system and draw the boundary.
  2. Identify the processes and what’s fixed in each (p, V, T, or adiabatic).
  3. Find the end states from the equation of state.
  4. Compute W along each path and ΔU from the end states.
  5. Get Q from the first law, and check that the residual Q−W−ΔU is zero.

Worked exampleHeating air under a piston with stops

2 L of air at 150 kPa and 300 K (3.4843 g) sits under a free piston. It’s heated at constant pressure to 500 K, when the piston reaches stops, then heated at constant volume to 700 K.

  1. Constant pressure: V2​=2⋅500/300=3.333 L. W=150000⋅0.001333=200.0 J. ΔU=0.0034843⋅718⋅200=500.3 J. Q=700.3 J.
  2. Constant volume: W=0, ΔU=Q=500.3 J. Final pressure 210.0 kPa.
  3. Totals: Q=1200.7 J, W=200.0 J, ΔU=1000.7 J =mcv​(700−300). The residual is zero in every step.
  4. An Otto-like cycle (adiabatic compression to 0.5 L, constant-volume heating by 400 K, adiabatic expansion, constant-volume cooling): net Q = net W = 425.73 J and ΔU=0 around the cycle.

Exercise 1A rigid tank

A rigid 50 L tank holds air at 100 kPa and 20 °C. A 200 W heater runs for 2 minutes and the tank loses 4 kJ of heat to the room meanwhile. Find the final temperature and pressure.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. m=pV/(RT)=100000⋅0.05/(287⋅293.15)=0.05943 kg.
  2. Net heat: 200⋅120−4000=20000 J. Rigid tank, no boundary work. The electric heater’s input counts as electrical work done on the system, W=−24 kJ, with Q=−4 kJ. Either way ΔU=20 kJ.
  3. ΔT=20000/(0.05943⋅718)=468.7 K, so T2​=761.8 K.
  4. p2​=100⋅761.8/293.15=259.9 kPa.

10.05.title: The first law for open systems
10.05.html:
Most energy machines have fluid flowing through them: air through a jet engine, steam through a turbine, water through a pump, refrigerant through a heat pump. We can’t follow a fixed lump of mass through them easily, so we draw a fixed control volume around the machine and keep account of energy carried in and out by the flow. In steady operation the result is one of the most useful equations in engineering.

Flow work and enthalpy

Pushing fluid into a control volume takes work: a slug of volume V pushed in against pressure p needs pV, or pv per kilogram. This flow work always accompanies the internal energy u carried in, so the natural combination is the enthalpy, h=u+pv.

The steady-flow energy equation

For one inlet (1) and one outlet (2) with mass flow m˙, steady operation:

Q˙​−W˙=m˙[(h2​−h1​)+2V22​−V12​​+g(z2​−z1​)].

W˙ is shaft power out; flow work is already inside h.

Typical devices

  • Nozzle: no work, nearly adiabatic. The enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy: V2​=V12​+2(h1​−h2​)​.
  • Turbine: adiabatic, kinetic energy changes small. W˙=m˙(h1​−h2​).
  • Compressor or pump: the same with work in. For a pump with liquid, h2​−h1​≈vΔp.
  • Throttle valve: no work, no heat, so h2​=h1​. An ideal gas leaves at the same temperature; a real fluid can cool sharply (10.15).
  • Heat exchanger: no work; heat lost by one stream equals heat gained by the other.

Orders of magnitude: 1 K of temperature in water is 4186 J/kg; 1 m of height is 9.81 J/kg; a speed of 45 m/s is 1000 J/kg. Kinetic and potential terms matter only in nozzles, diffusers and hydropower (10.07).

For an ideal gas flowing through a reversible adiabatic device, T2​/T1​=(p2​/p1​)(k−1)/k (10.10 covers real devices).

Worked exampleNozzle, turbine and compressor

Air with cp​=1005 J/(kg K), k=1.4.

  1. Nozzle: 500 K, 300 kPa, 30 m/s in, expanding isentropically to 100 kPa. T2​=500⋅(1/3)0.2857=365.36 K, so V2​=302+2⋅1005⋅134.64​=521.1 m/s. The energy residual is zero.
  2. Turbine: 2 kg/s from 1200 K and 1 MPa to 100 kPa. Exit 621.7 K, power 1162.3 kW.
  3. Compressor: 2 kg/s from 300 K and 100 kPa to 1 MPa. Exit 579.0 K, power absorbed 560.8 kW.
  4. Together they deliver 601.5 kW: the heart of a gas turbine (10.13).
  5. Throttle: h2​=h1​ gives zero power residual, and for an ideal gas no temperature change.

Exercise 1A water pump

A pump lifts 20 kg/s of water from 100 kPa to 1.5 MPa (v=0.001 m³/kg). Neglecting heat loss and velocity changes, what power does it need if it’s ideal? What temperature rise would friction cause if the pump were only 70 % efficient?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Ideal: W˙=m˙vΔp=20⋅0.001⋅1.4×106=28.0 kW.
  2. Actual: 28.0/0.7=40.0 kW. The extra 12.0 kW is dissipated into the water.
  3. ΔT=12000/(20⋅4186)=0.14 K. Pump losses barely warm the water, so measuring that rise needs very precise thermometers.

10.06.title: Pure substances and phase change
10.06.html:
Put a pan of water on the stove. It warms until it reaches 100 °C, then stays at 100 °C for a long time while it boils. All that energy goes into turning liquid into vapour, not into raising the temperature. Up a mountain the water boils at a lower temperature; in a pressure cooker at a higher one. Steam is far from an ideal gas, so engineers use property tables, and these days property libraries, to analyse boilers, turbines and heat pumps.

Phases and saturation

At a given pressure, liquid water boils at one saturation temperature Tsat​(p); equivalently each temperature has a saturation pressure. Between the saturated liquid state (f) and the saturated vapour state (g), the substance is a wet mixture whose temperature and pressure stay fixed while it boils. Beyond g it’s superheated vapour; below f, compressed liquid.

In the two-phase region p and T aren’t independent, so they can’t fix the state together. The quality x, the mass fraction of vapour, is the second property:

v=vf​+x(vg​−vf​),h=hf​+xhfg​,s=sf​+x(sg​−sf​).

Solving for x from any one known property gives the rest.

Reading tables in code

A saturation table lists psat​, vf​, vg​, hf​, hg​, sf​, sg​ at chosen temperatures. Between rows, interpolate. Linear interpolation is fine for h and s, but psat​ and vg​ change exponentially with temperature (the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, lnp≈A−B/T). Interpolating lnp against 1/T is far more accurate.

The latent heat hfg​ falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical point (374 °C, 22.06 MPa), where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable.

Worked exampleUsing the table

Saturation table for water from 10 to 300 °C (IAPWS-95 values).

  1. The interpolation function reproduces every tabulated row exactly.
  2. Between rows, compared with IAPWS-95: at 45 °C, psat​=9.5895 kPa (true 9.595), hf​=188.44 kJ/kg (188.435), vg​=15.262 m³/kg (15.252). At 150 °C: 475.78 kPa (476.17) and hf​=632.32 (632.18).
  3. Wet steam at 100 °C with x=0.9: v=1.5047 m³/kg, h=419.17+0.9⋅2256.40=2449.93 kJ/kg, s=6.7494 kJ/(kg K).
  4. Recovering the quality from h gives 0.9 exactly.

Exercise 1A rigid tank of wet steam

A rigid 0.5 m³ tank contains 2 kg of water at 120 °C. What’s the quality, and how much is vapour by mass and by volume?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=0.5/2=0.25 m³/kg. At 120 °C, vf​=0.001060 and vg​=0.8912 m³/kg, so it’s a wet mixture.
  2. x=(0.25−0.00106)/(0.8912−0.00106)=0.2797.
  3. Vapour mass: 0.2797⋅2=0.559 kg, occupying 0.559⋅0.8912=0.4985 m³, so 99.7 % of the volume. The liquid is only 1.44 kg in about 1.5 litres.

10.07.title: Pumped-storage hydropower
10.07.html:
Solar panels produce most at midday in summer; demand peaks on winter evenings. Storing electricity at grid scale is hard, and over 90 % of the world’s grid storage is one old idea: pump water uphill when power is cheap, let it run back through a turbine when power is scarce. Switzerland, with lakes hundreds of metres above each other, has some of the largest schemes in Europe. The thermodynamics is the first law with gravitational potential energy.

Energy stored

Lifting a volume V of water through a head h stores

E=ρghV.

It’s linear in both head and volume. One kilowatt-hour, 3.6×106 J, needs 3.6×106/(ρgh) m³ of water: 1.22 m³ falling 300 m, or 367 m³ falling 1 m. That’s why pumped storage needs mountains. A flat-land scheme would need a lake the size of a city.

Power is the flow rate times the head: P=ηρgQh, so a 900 MW plant at 300 m head moves about 340 m³ of water every second.

Round-trip efficiency

Every conversion loses something.

  • Generating: turbine (about 92 %), generator (98 %), and penstock friction, which takes a head hf​ off the available head.
  • Pumping: pump (about 91 %), motor (98 %), and the pump must deliver h+hf​.

Friction head follows Darcy-Weisbach, hf​=fDL​2gV2​, so penstocks are built several metres in diameter to keep the speed low. Multiplying the efficiencies gives the round trip, typically 75–82 %. About a fifth of the electricity is lost, but storing it is worth far more when the price difference between night and peak, or summer and winter, is large enough.

Worked exampleAn Alpine plant

Assumed round numbers loosely modelled on a large Alpine scheme: 25 million m³ upper reservoir, 300 m mean head, 900 MW, two penstocks 1.4 km long and 7 m in diameter.

  1. Stored energy: 1000⋅9.81⋅300⋅25×106=7.358×1013 J =20.44 GWh.
  2. Flow at full power: Q=P/(ρgh⋅0.90)=340 m³/s, 170 m³/s per penstock, about 4.4 m/s.
  3. Friction head: 2.38 m, only 0.79 % of the head.
  4. Generating efficiency 0.92⋅0.98⋅(1−0.0079)=0.894; pumping 0.91⋅0.98/(1+0.0079)=0.885; round trip 0.791.
  5. It returns 18.28 GWh for 23.10 GWh pumped in: 20.3 hours at full power.

Exercise 1Is it worth it?

A plant buys electricity at 40 CHF/MWh at night and sells at 120 CHF/MWh at the evening peak, with a round-trip efficiency of 0.79. What’s the margin per MWh sold, and what’s the minimum price ratio that breaks even? Also find the energy stored in a smaller reservoir of 2 million m³ at 500 m head.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Each MWh sold needs 1/0.79=1.266 MWh bought, costing 40/0.79=50.63 CHF.
  2. Margin: 120−50.63=69.37 CHF per MWh, before maintenance and grid fees.
  3. Break-even when sell/buy price =1/0.79=1.266.
  4. Smaller reservoir: 1000⋅9.81⋅500⋅2×106=9.81×1012 J =2.725 GWh. The higher head partly makes up for the much smaller volume.

10.08.title: The second law and the Carnot limit
10.08.html:
The first law says energy is conserved. It doesn’t say which way things go. A hot coffee cools in a cold room; it never spontaneously gets hotter. A car’s engine turns at most about 40 % of its fuel energy into work, not because engineers are careless but because nature sets a ceiling. The second law of thermodynamics is that ceiling, and the Carnot efficiency puts a number on it.

Two statements

  • Kelvin-Planck: no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and turn it all into work. Every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder sink.
  • Clausius: heat can’t flow from cold to hot on its own. A refrigerator needs work input.

The two are equivalent: a device violating one can be combined with an ordinary engine or fridge to violate the other.

The Carnot efficiency

A reversible engine between a hot reservoir at Th​ and a cold one at Tc​ (in kelvin) has efficiency

ηCarnot​=1−Th​Tc​​.

No engine working between the same two reservoirs can do better, and all reversible ones do exactly this well. In general, for any cycle the Clausius inequality holds:

∮TδQ​≤0,

with equality only for reversible cycles. On a T-s diagram a reversible cycle’s heat input is the area under its top, and its net work the enclosed area. The Carnot cycle is a rectangle, the shape that uses the temperature limits best. Any other shape between the same limits takes in heat below Th​ or rejects it above Tc​, and does worse.

The practical lesson is: raise Th​ (hotter combustion, superheated steam, better turbine blade alloys) and lower Tc​ (cold river water, cooling towers). A 150 °C geothermal source can never exceed 29.5 % however clever the machine.

Worked exampleNo shape beats the rectangle

  1. Between 300 K and 900 K the Carnot limit is 1−300/900=0.6667.
  2. A rectangle on the T-s diagram reproduces it to machine precision.
  3. 20 000 random reversible cycles drawn inside the same band: the best manages 0.5330, and every one stays below the Carnot limit for its own temperature extremes.
  4. Real limits: a coal plant with 565 °C steam and a 25 °C river, 64.4 % (real plants reach about 45 %); an engine with 2300 K peak gas and 300 K air, 87.0 %; geothermal at 150 °C, 29.5 %.

Exercise 1Check an inventor’s claim

An inventor says her engine takes 1000 kJ from a reservoir at 500 K, delivers 450 kJ of work and rejects 550 kJ to the surroundings at 300 K. Is it possible? Check both the efficiency and the Clausius inequality.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The first law is satisfied: 1000=450+550.
  2. Claimed efficiency 450/1000=0.45; Carnot limit 1−300/500=0.40. Impossible.
  3. Clausius: ∮δQ/T=1000/500−550/300=2.000−1.833=+0.167 kJ/K, which is greater than zero, so the cycle violates the second law.
  4. To be possible it would need to reject at least 1000⋅300/500=600 kJ.

10.09.title: Entropy
10.09.html:
Mix hot and cold water in a shower and you get warm water. Energy is perfectly conserved, yet something has been lost: you can’t unmix them, and you’ve thrown away the chance to run an engine between the hot and cold supplies. Entropy is the property that measures that loss. It increases in every real process and stays constant only in ideal reversible ones.

Definition

For a reversible process, entropy changes by

dS=TδQrev​​.

Entropy is a property: its change between two states is the same whatever the process, reversible or not. To calculate it, invent any convenient reversible path. For an incompressible liquid or solid with specific heat c,

Δs=clnT1​T2​​.

Entropy generation

For a real process the balance gains a generation term that can’t be negative:

ΔSsystem​=∫Tb​δQ​+Sgen​,Sgen​≥0,

where Tb​ is the temperature at the boundary where the heat crosses. For a steady-flow device, ∑m˙out​sout​−∑m˙in​sin​=∑Q˙​/Tb​+S˙gen​.

Sources of generation: heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, friction, mixing, unrestrained expansion, electrical resistance. Engineering for efficiency is largely hunting these down.

Mixing two streams

In an insulated mixer, the energy balance gives the exit temperature T3​=(m˙1​T1​+m˙2​T2​)/(m˙1​+m˙2​). The hot stream loses entropy, the cold one gains more than that, and

S˙gen​=m˙1​clnT1​T3​​+m˙2​clnT2​T3​​≥0,

zero only when T1​=T2​. Because ln is concave, the weighted log of the mean temperature is always larger than the weighted mean of the logs.

Worked exampleA shower

0.08 kg/s of hot water at 60 °C mixes with 0.04 kg/s of cold at 15 °C; c=4.186 kJ/(kg K).

  1. Exit temperature: (0.08⋅333.15+0.04⋅288.15)/0.12=318.15 K =45.00 °C.
  2. Hot stream: 0.08⋅4.186ln(318.15/333.15)=−0.015428 kW/K. Cold: 0.04⋅4.186ln(318.15/288.15)=+0.016584 kW/K.
  3. S˙gen​=1.1557 W/K. With surroundings at T0​=288.15 K the lost work potential is T0​S˙gen​=333.01 W.
  4. 100 000 random mixings never give negative generation.
  5. Heating 1 kg of water from 15 to 60 °C changes its entropy by 0.60744 kJ/K whatever the process. From a 60 °C reservoir, the reservoir loses 4.186⋅45/333.15, so 0.04202 kJ/K is generated.

Exercise 1An insulated bucket

Pour 1 kg of water at 80 °C into 2 kg at 20 °C in an insulated bucket. Find the final temperature, the entropy generated and the lost work with surroundings at 20 °C.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. T3​=(353.15+2⋅293.15)/3=313.15 K =40 °C.
  2. Hot: 4.186ln(313.15/353.15)=−0.50320 kJ/K. Cold: 2⋅4.186ln(313.15/293.15)=+0.55253 kJ/K.
  3. Sgen​=0.04933 kJ/K, positive as it must be.
  4. Lost work T0​Sgen​=293.15⋅0.04933=14.46 kJ: an ideal engine running between the two buckets could have produced that before they reached 40 °C.

10.10.title: Isentropic efficiency
10.10.html:
A bicycle pump gets hot when you use it hard. Part of that is the ideal temperature rise of compressing air, and part is friction and turbulence that a perfect machine wouldn’t have. Turbomachinery engineers separate the two with one number per machine, the isentropic efficiency. It compares the real compressor or turbine with an ideal reversible, adiabatic one working between the same pressures.

The ideal reference

An adiabatic reversible process has constant entropy. For an ideal gas with constant specific heats,

Δs=cp​lnT1​T2​​−Rlnp1​p2​​=0⇒T1​T2s​​=(p1​p2​​)(k−1)/k,

with k=cp​/cv​≈1.4 for air.

Definitions

A real compressor needs more work than the ideal one; a real turbine delivers less:

ηc​=h2​−h1​h2s​−h1​​,ηt​=h3​−h4s​h3​−h4​​.

Both put the ideal work in the “better” place, so both are below 1. With constant cp​, h differences are cp​ times temperature differences, so the actual compressor exit temperature is

T2​=T1​+ηc​T2s​−T1​​.

On an h-s diagram the ideal process is a vertical line; the real one leans to the right, because friction generates entropy. Modern large compressors and turbines reach 85–92 %.

Worked exampleA gas-turbine compressor

Air enters at 20 °C and 1 bar; pressure ratio 8; ηc​=0.85; cp​=1.005, R=0.287 kJ/(kg K), so k=1.3997.

  1. T2s​=293.15⋅80.2857=530.87 K.
  2. T2​=293.15+(530.87−293.15)/0.85=572.82 K =299.7 °C.
  3. Work: 1.005⋅(572.82−293.15)=281.07 kJ/kg against 238.91 ideal.
  4. Entropy generated: 1.005ln(572.82/293.15)−0.287ln8=0.07644 kJ/(kg K). The code checks that it’s positive for every efficiency below 1 and that η=1 recovers the isentropic state.
  5. Turbine from 1400 K over the same ratio at 90 %: T4s​=773.09 K, T4​=835.78 K, work 567.04 kJ/kg.

Exercise 1From measurements back to efficiency

A test rig measures that the compressor above (20 °C in, ratio 8) actually delivers air at 320 °C. What’s its isentropic efficiency, and how much extra work per kg goes into friction compared with the ideal?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. T2​=593.15 K; T2s​=530.87 K as before.
  2. ηc​=(530.87−293.15)/(593.15−293.15)=237.72/300.00=0.7924.
  3. Extra work: 1.005⋅(593.15−530.87)=62.59 kJ/kg, which ends up as a hotter exit gas.

10.11.title: Exergy
10.11.html:
A litre of water at 90 °C and a litre of seawater at 15 °C hold huge amounts of internal energy, but only the first is useful: you can run an engine between it and the surroundings. Exergy is the maximum work obtainable from a system as it comes into equilibrium with the environment, the dead state at T0​, p0​. Unlike energy, exergy is destroyed in every real process, and that destruction is what engineers should be minimising.

Exergy of heat and of a flowing stream

Heat Q delivered at temperature T could at best drive a Carnot engine rejecting to T0​:

XQ​=Q(1−TT0​​).

1000 kJ at 90 °C is worth only 206.5 kJ of work; at 1500 °C, 837.5 kJ. Same energy, very different quality.

For a stream (ignoring kinetic and potential energy), the specific flow exergy is

ψ=(h−h0​)−T0​(s−s0​).

The exergy balance and Gouy-Stodola

In any device, exergy in = exergy out + exergy destroyed, and the destruction is

X˙dest​=T0​S˙gen​≥0,

the Gouy-Stodola theorem. A heat exchanger with no heat leaks has a first-law efficiency of 100 %, yet can destroy most of the exergy given up by the hot stream if the two streams are far apart in temperature. The second-law efficiency, exergy recovered over exergy supplied, shows that.

Worked exampleA water heat exchanger

Dead state 15 °C. Hot water at 1 kg/s cools from 90 to 50 °C; cold water at 1.5 kg/s enters at 10 °C; c=4.186 kJ/(kg K).

  1. Duty Q=4.186⋅40=167.44 kW; the cold stream leaves at 10+40/1.5=36.67 °C.
  2. Exergy given by the hot stream: 26.678 kW. Gained by the cold stream: 4.596 kW.
  3. Destroyed: 22.081 kW, equal to T0​S˙gen​ to machine precision.
  4. Second-law efficiency 4.596/26.678=0.172. The cold stream, warmed to only 37 °C, can’t store the quality of 90 °C heat.

Exercise 1Electric heating

An electric heater supplies 10 kW of heat to a room at 20 °C on a 0 °C day. What’s the exergy of that heat, and the second-law efficiency of the heater? What does that say about heat pumps?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Electricity is pure exergy: 10 kW in.
  2. Exergy of the heat with T0​=273.15 K: 10(1−273.15/293.15)=0.682 kW.
  3. Second-law efficiency 0.682/10=6.8 %, even though the first-law efficiency is 100 %.
  4. A device that used 0.682 kW of work to pump heat in would be ideal: that’s a Carnot heat pump with COP 14.7. Real heat pumps with a COP of 3–4 are far from perfect but still 3–4 times better than resistance heating.

10.12.title: Otto and Diesel cycles
10.12.html:
A petrol engine sparks its mixture at the top of the stroke and burns it almost instantly; a diesel squeezes air so hard it gets hot enough to ignite fuel sprayed in as the piston moves down. Both are messy in reality: friction, heat losses, real combustion. The air-standard cycles strip that away, treating the working fluid as air in a closed cycle with heat added and removed, and they explain the main design trends.

The Otto cycle

  1. 1→2: isentropic compression by the compression ratio r=v1​/v2​.
  2. 2→3: heat added at constant volume (the spark).
  3. 3→4: isentropic expansion.
  4. 4→1: heat rejected at constant volume.

With constant specific heats the efficiency depends only on r:

ηOtto​=1−rk−11​.

Higher compression means higher efficiency, but petrol engines are limited to about 10–13 by knock, auto-ignition of the end gas.

The Diesel cycle

Heat is added at constant pressure while the piston moves out, until the cutoff ratio rc​=v3​/v2​:

ηDiesel​=1−rk−11​k(rc​−1)rck​−1​.

The bracket is always above 1, so at the same r the Diesel is less efficient. But diesels compress only air, so knock isn’t a problem and they run at r = 15–22, which wins overall.

Worked exampleIntegrating the loop

Air, cv​=0.718, R=0.287 kJ/(kg K), k=1.3997, starting at 300 K and 100 kPa. The code integrates ∮pdv numerically and compares with the formulas.

  1. Otto with 1200 kJ/kg added: r=8, 0.5645 (peak 2360 K, 6.29 MPa); r=10, 0.6016; r=12, 0.6296. Integration agrees to five digits.
  2. Diesel, r=18, rc​=2: 0.6313, peak 1905 K at 5.72 MPa.
  3. Same r=10: Otto 0.6016, Diesel 0.5337.

Exercise 1Matching a diesel

What compression ratio would an Otto cycle need to match the Diesel’s 0.6313? Why can’t a petrol engine simply use it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 1−r1−k=0.6313⇒r=(1−0.6313)1/(1−k)=0.3687−2.502=12.14.
  2. That’s at the edge of what petrol engines tolerate. Premium fuels and direct injection allow about 13, but in a premixed charge the unburnt end gas would auto-ignite (knock) at higher ratios, so real petrol engines run lower.
  3. Real engine efficiencies are well below air-standard values: about 35–40 % for petrol and 45–50 % for large diesels.

10.13.title: The Brayton cycle
10.13.html:
Every jet engine and every gas turbine power station runs the same loop: squeeze air, burn fuel in it, expand the hot gas through a turbine that drives the compressor, and use what’s left as thrust or shaft power. The ideal version is the Brayton cycle. Its main lesson is how much the compressor costs: often half of what the turbine makes, so component efficiencies matter enormously.

The ideal cycle

  1. 1→2: isentropic compression by the pressure ratio rp​.
  2. 2→3: heat added at constant pressure (the combustor).
  3. 3→4: isentropic expansion.
  4. 4→1: heat rejected at constant pressure (exhaust).

With air as an ideal gas with constant cp​,

ηBrayton​=1−rp(1−k)/k​.

Like Otto, it rises with pressure ratio only.

Real components

With isentropic efficiencies ηc​ and ηt​ the compressor needs more work and the turbine gives less:

wnet​=cp​(T3​−T4​)−cp​(T2​−T1​).

The back-work ratio wc​/wt​ is 40–60 % for gas turbines, compared with 1–2 % for steam plants, where the pump only pushes liquid. A few points of component efficiency therefore swing the net output a lot. Net work peaks at a moderate pressure ratio and efficiency at a higher one. Hotter turbine inlets (with blade cooling and single-crystal superalloys) raise both.

Worked exampleA simple gas turbine

Air at 300 K, rp​=8, turbine inlet 1400 K, ηc​=0.85, ηt​=0.90, cp​=1.005 kJ/(kg K), k=1.3997.

  1. Ideal efficiency: 1−8−0.2856=0.4478.
  2. Real: T2​=586.20 K, T4​=835.78 K.
  3. Compressor 287.64, turbine 567.04, net 279.40 kJ/kg; heat in 817.86 kJ/kg.
  4. Efficiency 0.3416, back-work ratio 0.507. The energy balance closes: heat in minus net work equals heat rejected.
  5. Sweeping rp​: net work peaks at rp​=9.3 (280.6 kJ/kg); efficiency peaks at 22.6 (0.3977). For the ideal cycle, maximum work is at (T3​/T1​)k/(2(k−1))=14.84.

Exercise 1A hotter turbine

Raise the turbine inlet temperature of the example to 1600 K and keep everything else. Find the efficiency, net work and back-work ratio, and the power from 100 kg/s of air in both cases.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Compressor work is unchanged at 287.64 kJ/kg.
  2. Turbine: T4​=1600−0.9(1600−1600/1.8115)=955.2 K; wt​=648.05 kJ/kg; net 360.41 kJ/kg.
  3. Heat in 1.005(1600−586.20)=1018.86 kJ/kg; efficiency 0.3537; back-work ratio 0.444.
  4. At 100 kg/s: 27.94 MW at 1400 K, 36.04 MW at 1600 K, 29 % more power from the same machine size.

10.14.title: The Rankine steam cycle
10.14.html:
Most of the world’s electricity, from coal, gas combined cycles, nuclear, geothermal and solar thermal plants, comes from steam turbines. The loop is the Rankine cycle: pump water to high pressure, boil and superheat it, expand the steam through a turbine, condense it back to liquid. Because it pumps a liquid instead of compressing a gas, the pump costs almost nothing.

The four steps

  1. Pump (1→2): liquid from the condenser to boiler pressure. Work wp​=vΔp, small because liquid volume is tiny.
  2. Boiler (2→3): heat at constant pressure, through the liquid region, across the dome and into superheat.
  3. Turbine (3→4): expansion to condenser pressure, ideally isentropic.
  4. Condenser (4→1): heat rejected at constant pressure, usually to a river, the sea or a cooling tower.

Efficiency is η=(wt​−wp​)/qin​. Steam isn’t an ideal gas, so states come from tables: find s3​ at the turbine inlet, then the exit quality x4​=(s3​−sf​)/(sg​−sf​) at the condenser.

Superheat and reheat

Raising the steam temperature raises the average temperature of heat addition, which pushes efficiency up towards Carnot. It also keeps the turbine exhaust drier. Below about 88 % quality, water droplets erode the last-stage blades. Reheat expands the steam part-way, sends it back to the boiler, and expands it again: efficiency rises a little and the exhaust gets much drier.

Worked exampleA 10 MPa plant

Boiler 10 MPa, condenser 10 kPa (45.81 °C), steam at 500 °C. Steam values come from small IAPWS-95 tables in the code; h3​=3375.13 kJ/kg, s3​=6.5995 kJ/(kg K).

  1. Pump: 0.0010103⋅(10000−10)=10.09 kJ/kg.
  2. Ideal turbine: x4​=(6.5995−0.6492)/(8.1488−0.6492)=0.7934, h4​=2089.7 kJ/kg, wt​=1285.4 kJ/kg.
  3. Heat in 3173.2 kJ/kg, out 1897.9 kJ/kg: efficiency 0.4019 (Carnot between the same extremes: 0.5875). The energy balance closes.
  4. With an 85 % turbine: 0.3411, exit quality 0.8740.
  5. With reheat at 2 MPa to 500 °C: 0.4167, exit quality 0.9046. With 85 % turbines: 0.3602 and 0.9744.

Exercise 1Sizing a power plant

A plant on the ideal reheat cycle above must deliver 500 MW net. Find the steam flow, the heat rejected in the condenser and the cooling water flow if the river water may warm by only 10 K.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Net work: 1555.9−10.09=1545.8 kJ/kg. Steam flow 500000/1545.8=323.5 kg/s.
  2. Heat rejected: 323.5⋅2164.0=700.0 MW, more than the electricity produced.
  3. Cooling water: 700000/(4.186⋅10)=16721 kg/s, about 17 m³ of river water every second. That’s why big plants sit on rivers or coasts, or use cooling towers.

10.15.title: Heat pumps
10.15.html:
A heat pump is a refrigerator turned inside out: it takes heat from cold outdoor air or ground and delivers it, with the compressor’s work added, into a house. One kilowatt-hour of electricity can deliver three to five of heat, which is why heat pumps have become the default heating in new Swiss and European homes. Many now use propane, R290, a natural refrigerant with negligible global warming potential.

The vapour-compression cycle

  1. Evaporator (4→1): cold liquid-vapour mixture boils at low pressure, absorbing heat from outdoor air at Te​, below outdoor temperature.
  2. Compressor (1→2): saturated vapour compressed to the condensing pressure, with isentropic efficiency ηc​.
  3. Condenser (2→3): vapour condenses at Tc​, above the supply water temperature, releasing heat into the heating water.
  4. Expansion valve (3→4): throttling at constant enthalpy, h4​=h3​.

The heating coefficient of performance is

COPh​=wqout​​=h2​−h1​h2​−h3​​,COPCarnot​=Tc​−Te​Tc​​.

COP exceeds 1 because the work moves heat rather than creating it. The Carnot value is the second-law ceiling. It falls as the temperature lift grows, so heat pumps love mild weather and low supply temperatures: floor heating at 35 °C beats radiators at 55 °C.

Getting the states

The saturated states come from a table. Propane leaves the compressor only slightly superheated, so modelling the vapour along the condensing isobar with constant cp​, s=sg​+cp​ln(T/Tc​), reproduces CoolProp’s isentropic exit enthalpy to within 0.02 kJ/kg.

Worked exampleFloor heating near freezing

Outdoor air 0 °C (evaporate at −5 °C), floor heating at 35 °C (condense at 40 °C), ηc​=0.70.

  1. h1​=569.30, h3​=307.15 kJ/kg; isentropic exit 45.33 °C, h2s​=626.27 kJ/kg (CoolProp: 626.28).
  2. Pressure ratio 3.37.
  3. Isentropic COP 5.601; with ηc​=0.70, COP 4.221; Carnot 6.959.
  4. Floor heating against radiators (55 °C supply) at outdoor −15/−5/2/7/15 °C: 3.11/3.78/4.43/5.04/6.46 against 2.26/2.61/2.92/3.19/3.74. Every value stays below Carnot.

Exercise 1Floor heating or radiators?

A house needs 8 kW of heat when it’s 0 °C outside. Find the electric power with floor heating (condense at 40 °C) and with radiators (condense at 60 °C), evaporating at −5 °C in both cases.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Floor heating: COP 4.221, so 8/4.221=1.895 kW of electricity.
  2. Radiators: the model gives COP 2.822, so 8/2.822=2.835 kW. The Carnot COP here is 333.15/65=5.125.
  3. Radiators need 50 % more electricity. Old houses often get bigger radiators when converting, so they can run at lower water temperatures.

10.16.title: Real gases and van der Waals
10.16.html:
The ideal gas law works beautifully for air at room conditions. Squeeze CO2 into a fire extinguisher or a supercritical-CO2 power loop and it fails badly: molecules take up space and attract each other. In 1873 Johannes van der Waals added two corrections to pv=RT. His equation is too crude for design work, but it’s the simplest model that predicts condensation and a critical point, and the ideas behind modern cubic equations of state come straight from it.

The equation

Per mole,

p=v−bRT​−v2a​.
  • b is the volume the molecules themselves occupy, so the free volume is v−b.
  • a/v2 is the pressure lost to attraction between molecules, which grows as they crowd together.

For CO2, a=0.3640 Pa m⁶/mol² and b=4.267×10−5 m³/mol. The compressibility factor Z=pv/RT measures departure from ideal behaviour. As p→0, v grows huge, both corrections vanish and Z→1.

Solving for volume

Given p and T, the equation is a cubic in v:

pv3−(pb+RT)v2+av−ab=0.

Above the critical temperature it has one real root. Below it, in a pressure range, it has three: liquid (smallest), vapour (largest), and an unstable middle one.

The critical point and Maxwell’s construction

The critical isotherm has a horizontal inflection: Tc​=8a/(27Rb), pc​=a/(27b2). Below Tc​ the isotherm wiggles, which a real fluid never does. Maxwell showed that the real saturation pressure is the horizontal line that cuts off equal areas above and below the loop, because liquid and vapour in equilibrium must have equal Gibbs energy.

Worked exampleCO2

  1. Critical point from a and b: 304.00 K and 7.404 MPa (real CO2: 304.13 K, 7.377 MPa). The model predicts Zc​=3/8=0.375; real CO2 has 0.274, one sign of its limits.
  2. At 350 K: Z = 0.99997 at 1 kPa, 0.99716 at 0.1 MPa, 0.97107 at 1 MPa and 0.83972 at 5 MPa, where v=0.48873 L/mol against 0.58201 for an ideal gas.
  3. Maxwell construction at 280 K: psat​=5.2843 MPa (real CO2: 4.160 MPa), liquid 80.88 and vapour 265.4 cm³/mol.

Exercise 1A CO2 cylinder

A 10 litre cylinder holds 2 kg of CO2 at 350 K (above critical, so one phase). Find the pressure from the ideal gas law and from van der Waals.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Moles: 2/0.04401=45.44 mol, so v=0.010/45.44=2.2005×10−4 m³/mol.
  2. Ideal: p=RT/v=13.22 MPa.
  3. Van der Waals: p=2.2005×10−4−4.267×10−58.3145⋅350​−(2.2005×10−4)20.3640​=8.89 MPa.
  4. The ideal gas law overestimates by about 49 %. For a pressure vessel design you’d use an accurate equation of state such as Span-Wagner, but van der Waals points the right way.

10.17.title: Psychrometrics
10.17.html:
31 °C in Bali feels oppressive; 31 °C on a dry Zurich summer day feels pleasant. The difference is water vapour. Psychrometrics, the thermodynamics of moist air, tells an engineer how much water the air carries, when it will condense on a cold surface, and how much of an air conditioner’s work goes into drying the air rather than cooling it. In the tropics that’s most of it.

Describing moist air

Treat moist air as a mixture of dry air and water vapour, both ideal gases at total pressure p, with vapour partial pressure pv​.

  • Relative humidity ϕ=pv​/psat​(T): how close the air is to saturation.
  • Humidity ratio ω=0.622pv​/(p−pv​): kg of water per kg of dry air. It depends on the total pressure, which is lower in Zurich at 408 m than in Bali at sea level.
  • Dew point Td​: the temperature at which psat​(Td​)=pv​, where water starts to condense.
  • Enthalpy per kg of dry air: h=1.006T+ω(2501+1.86T) kJ/kg, with T in °C. The 2501 is the latent heat of vaporisation at 0 °C, and it dominates.

The saturation pressure here comes from the Magnus formula, psat​=610.94exp(T+243.0417.625T​) Pa (over liquid water), accurate to about 0.1 % between −40 and 50 °C. It inverts exactly, which gives the dew point.

Air conditioning in the tropics

To bring humid air to a comfortable state, an air conditioner cools it below the target’s dew point, so the excess water condenses on the coil and drains away, then (in good systems) reheats it slightly. The latent load, the water removed, often exceeds the sensible load.

Worked exampleBali against Zurich

  1. Denpasar afternoon, 31 °C, 75 %, 101.3 kPa: ω=21.37 g/kg, dew point 26.05 °C, h=85.86 kJ/kg.
  2. Zurich July afternoon, 25 °C, 50 %, 96.6 kPa: 10.35 g/kg, dew point 13.86 °C, h=51.51 kJ/kg.
  3. Zurich January morning, 0 °C, 85 %: 3.36 g/kg, dew point −2.22 °C (over liquid water).
  4. The code checks that at 100 % humidity the dew point equals the air temperature.
  5. Air conditioning in Bali from 31 °C, 75 % to 24 °C, 50 %: cool to 12.94 °C and condense 12.09 g of water per kg of air. Cooling 48.76 kJ/kg and reheat 11.32 kJ/kg, against 7.04 kJ/kg if the air were dry.

Exercise 1Dry winter air in Zurich

Outdoor air at 0 °C and 85 % is heated to 21 °C indoors with no moisture added. What’s the indoor relative humidity? At what surface temperature does a window start to fog?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Vapour pressure: 0.85⋅610.94=519.3 Pa. Heating doesn’t change it.
  2. At 21 °C, psat​=2481.9 Pa, so RH =519.3/2481.9=20.9 %. That’s why heated rooms feel dry in winter.
  3. The dew point stays at −2.22 °C, so the window fogs only below that. With people, cooking and showers adding moisture, real indoor dew points are much higher, and cold window frames do fog.

10.18.title: Combustion and flame temperature
10.18.html:
A gas stove, a boiler, a turbine combustor and a rocket all release chemical energy by burning fuel. How hot the flame gets sets material limits, NOx emissions and engine efficiency. The adiabatic flame temperature is the temperature products reach if all the chemical energy goes into heating them, with no heat loss. It’s an energy balance with the enthalpy of formation included.

Stoichiometry

Methane burns completely with exactly enough air in

CH4​+2(O2​+3.76N2​)→CO2​+2H2​O+7.52N2​,

a stoichiometric air-fuel mass ratio of 17.12. The equivalence ratio ϕ is the actual fuel-air ratio over the stoichiometric one. With ϕ<1 (lean) excess O2 leaves in the exhaust. With ϕ>1 (rich) there isn’t enough oxygen, and CO and H2 appear. Here they’re split by the water-gas shift equilibrium CO2​+H2​⇌CO+H2​O.

The energy balance

With no heat or work, the enthalpy of the reactants equals the enthalpy of the products:

react∑​ni​hˉi​(T0​)=prod∑​nj​hˉj​(Tad​),

where each hˉ includes the enthalpy of formation. The code takes hˉ(T) from NASA 7-coefficient polynomials, the standard format used by combustion codes, and finds Tad​ by bisection. The same data give methane’s lower heating value of 50.03 MJ/kg.

The flame is hottest near stoichiometric. Lean, extra air soaks up heat; rich, part of the fuel’s energy stays locked in CO and H2. Real flames are about 100 K cooler, because at these temperatures CO2 and H2O partly dissociate. That shifts the peak slightly rich, which the next lesson covers.

Worked exampleMethane and air from 298 K

  1. Lower heating value: 50.03 MJ/kg.
  2. Tad​: φ 0.6, 1669.3 K; 0.8, 2015.0 K; 1.0, 2325.6 K; 1.1, 2232.3 K; 1.2, 2144.2 K; 1.4, 1981.3 K.
  3. At φ = 1.2, the shift equilibrium gives 0.581 CO2, 0.419 CO, 1.752 H2O and 0.248 H2 per mole of fuel. The atom balances check.
  4. The peak is 2325.6 K at φ = 1.00. A full equilibrium calculation with dissociation (Cantera, GRI-Mech 3.0) gives 2225 K at φ = 1.

Exercise 1A lean burner

A low-NOx boiler burner runs with 25 % excess air. What’s the equivalence ratio, the air-fuel mass ratio and the adiabatic flame temperature? Why run lean?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 25 % excess air means 1.25 times the stoichiometric air, so ϕ=1/1.25=0.8.
  2. Air-fuel ratio: 1.25⋅17.12=21.40 by mass.
  3. From the code, Tad​=2015.0 K, 311 K below the stoichiometric peak.
  4. Thermal NOx forms very strongly above about 1800 K, so a cooler lean flame cuts NOx dramatically. Excess air also makes sure all the CO burns out. The price is more hot exhaust carrying heat away.

10.19.title: Chemical equilibrium
10.19.html:
Heat CO2 enough and some of it falls apart into CO and O2. Cool it and they recombine. Which mixture does nature settle on at a given temperature and pressure? The answer is the second law again: at fixed T and p, a system reaches equilibrium when its Gibbs energy G=H−TS is at a minimum. That one principle underlies flame temperatures, catalytic converters, ammonia synthesis and the chemistry of rocket exhaust.

Gibbs energy of a mixture

For ideal gases at total pressure p, each species i with ni​ moles and mole fraction yi​ contributes

G=i∑​ni​[gˉ​i∘​(T)+RTlnp∘yi​p​],

where gˉ​∘=hˉ−Tsˉ∘ comes from the same NASA polynomials as the last lesson and p∘=1 bar. The logarithm is a mixing entropy term that always favours some of every species.

Minimising G

For CO2​⇌CO+21​O2​ starting from 1 mol CO2, everything depends on one extent of reaction ξ: 1−ξ CO2, ξ CO and ξ/2 O2. Plot G(ξ); the minimum is equilibrium. Because G is convex in ξ, a golden-section search finds it reliably. Bigger problems with many species use the same idea with Lagrange multipliers for the atom balances.

The equilibrium constant

Setting dG/dξ=0 gives the familiar form

Kp​=exp(−RTΔG∘​)=yCO2​​yCO​yO2​1/2​​(p∘p​)1/2,

where ΔG∘ is the standard Gibbs energy change of the reaction. Higher temperature makes ΔG∘ less positive and pushes the reaction forward. Higher pressure pushes it back, because dissociation increases the number of moles (Le Chatelier).

Worked exampleCO2 at 1 atm

  1. Dissociated fraction from Gibbs minimisation: 1500 K, 0.00036; 2000 K, 0.01499; 2500 K, 0.12926; 3000 K, 0.43736; 3500 K, 0.74925.
  2. The Kp​ method gives identical values; at 2500 K, Kp​=0.036816.
  3. At 2500 K the mixture is 81.79 % CO2, 12.14 % CO and 6.07 % O2 by moles.
  4. At 10 atm and 2500 K only 0.06236 dissociates.
  5. A Cantera calculation with the same species agrees to within 1 % (it uses a reference pressure of 1 atm rather than 1 bar).

Exercise 1Pressure and dissociation

At 3000 K, find the dissociated fraction of CO2 at 1 atm and 10 atm. Explain why rocket and engine designers care.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. 1 atm: ξ=0.4374. 10 atm: ξ=0.2410.
  2. Raising pressure tenfold cuts dissociation by almost half, as Le Chatelier predicts for a reaction that increases the moles from 1 to 1.5.
  3. Dissociation absorbs energy, so it caps flame temperature and leaves energy in CO and O2 rather than in heat. High-pressure combustion chambers in rockets and diesels suffer less of it. The CO recombines as gases cool through a nozzle or expansion stroke, releasing some energy back.

10.20.title: Switzerland's seasonal energy balance
10.20.html:
Switzerland gets much of its electricity from water, and the water arrives at the wrong time: snowmelt fills rivers and lakes in summer, while demand peaks in winter. Phasing out nuclear and adding solar, which also peaks in summer, widens that gap. This lesson puts the thermodynamics of the phase together, energy balances, storage and conversion efficiencies, into a national-scale monthly model. All numbers here are assumed round values of roughly the right size, for illustration, not official statistics.

The model

Each source and the demand get an annual total, in TWh, and a seasonal shape: twelve monthly weights 1+Acos(2π(m−mpeak​)/12), which average 1.

Item (assumed) TWh/year Seasonal swing Peak
Demand 60 ±15 % January
Run-of-river hydro 18 ±45 % July
Natural inflow to storage lakes 20 ±80 % July
Nuclear 18 or 0 ±10 % January
Other (biomass, waste, wind) 4 none
Solar PV variable ±60 % July

Balances

For each month, net = supply − demand. The annual sum is the net export (or, if negative, import). The seasonal storage needed is the largest swing in the cumulative level after taking out the annual average:

Lm​=k≤m∑​(netk​−12annual​),storage=mmax​Lm​−mmin​Lm​.

The storage lakes, worth roughly 8.8 TWh, already do exactly this with the natural inflow. Anything beyond them has to come from imports, new storage, or winter-heavy production.

Worked exampleFour scenarios

  1. Today-like (nuclear on, 6 TWh PV): +6.00 TWh a year but −7.85 TWh in the winter half; storage needed 10.85 TWh, 2.05 beyond the lakes.
  2. Nuclear off, 6 TWh PV: −12.00 TWh a year, −17.41 in winter.
  3. Nuclear off, 24 TWh PV: the year is back to +6.00 TWh, but winter is −11.77 and storage needed rises to 14.77 TWh, 5.97 beyond the lakes.
  4. Nuclear off, 34 TWh PV: +16.00 TWh a year, yet still 7.84 TWh beyond the lakes.
  5. In every case supply minus net export equals demand, and the storage level returns to its starting value.

Exercise 1Hydrogen as seasonal storage

In scenario 3 the extra 5.97 TWh of storage beyond the lakes is to come from summer electricity turned into hydrogen and back into winter electricity, with a 35 % round trip. How much summer electricity does that take, and how does it compare with pumped storage?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Summer input: 5.97/0.35=17.06 TWh, nearly as much as the extra solar added between scenarios 2 and 3.
  2. Losses: 17.06−5.97=11.09 TWh, mostly as heat in electrolysers and fuel cells or turbines. That heat could go into district heating to raise the useful output.
  3. Pumped storage returns about 79 % (lesson 10.07), but storing 6 TWh needs huge lakes: with the 300 m head of that example, about 7.3 km³ of water. That’s why the real Swiss plan mixes more winter production (Alpine solar, wind), raised dams, imports and some power-to-gas.
